Scaffold confounding and identification. Kapoor et al. (2026) show empirically that scaffold choice
can move scores by as much as model choice. When a new generation of models arrives alongside new
scaffolding strategies, observed improvements reflect both factors simultaneously, a general concern in LLM-
agent evaluation (Liu et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2024; Xie et al., 2024). We formalize this as an identification
problem: where model era and scaffold era are collinear, a shape change concentrated at specific difficulties
cannot be identified without additional assumptions, and moving to a no-scaffold benchmark eliminates
the confound by construction. Du et al. (2025) provide a related motivation: scalar accuracy can conceal
substantial variation in token efficiency across models with identical solve rates, illustrating that scalar
summaries hide structure that matters for downstream conclusions.
3 Data and Method
Figure 2 summarizes the design. We identify the effect on a no-scaffold benchmark, use CurveShift to
separate a level shift in ability from a hard-item shape change, and report the shape effect over a grid of
pinned discrimination with cluster bootstrap intervals.
3.1 Data
We assemble three public result matrices, each providing per-model per-item binary outcomes with difficulty
labels assigned by humans independently of the models under evaluation. This exogenous labeling avoids
the circularity that arises when difficulty is inferred from the same model population whose progress is being
measured. For METR the label is human completion time. Liu et al. (2026) report that latent item difficulty
is linear in its logarithm, which supports its use as a difficulty scale.
4</page><page num="6">Our estimand is retrospective and structural. We ask whether the transition at this fixed historical breakpoint
changed the shape of the difficulty-response curve, not whether the current frontier differs from the past.
The claim is therefore anchored to the 2024.70 transition rather than to the date of analysis, and it does
not depend on including the most recent models. A data window that straddles the breakpoint is what the
question requires. The variant in continuous time in Section 5 shows the hard-item effect is an ongoing trend
within the window, not a single step.

6</page><page num="12">LiveCodeBench breaks the collinearity by construction. It has no agentic scaffold, so there is no harness
era to confound with the model era. The hard-item era effect on LiveCodeBench isolates deployed model
capability, including native inference-time reasoning, from the contribution of any harness. The result of
Section 5 can therefore be read as a statement about models, not scaffolds.
The properties that make LiveCodeBench usable here are rare in combination. A benchmark must pair
dated models that straddle the reasoning era breakpoint with per-item outcomes, an exogenous difficulty
ordering, and the absence of an agentic scaffold. Few public benchmarks meet all four requirements at once.
The nearest alternatives each fail one condition: CodeElo (Quan et al., 2025) shares the Codeforces source
rather than adding an independent one, LiveBench (White et al., 2025) lacks a clean exogenous per-item
difficulty, practical code-generation suites such as BigCodeBench (Zhuo et al., 2025) do not provide the same
dated no-scaffold panel with contest difficulty, and dated math competition sets such as Omni-MATH (Gao
et al., 2025) do not publish a per-item matrix across dated models.
We tried one such math panel directly, and the way it fails is itself informative. On the MathArena 2025
contests (Balunovic et al., 2025), models answer without a scaffold and the contest origin gives a difficulty
ordering, so two of the four conditions are met. The other two are not. The only per-item difficulty is
the problem index, an endogenous proxy rather than an exogenous ordering, and the era coverage is nearly
absent: these panels evaluate the models available when each contest is released, so the pre-era side holds
zero to two models per contest. With the pre-era hard-item cells almost empty, the post-by-hard contrast
has no pre-era support, and the era coefficient is not defined on these data before any model is fit. A fit run
anyway returns a degenerate estimate near zero, which reflects this missing support rather than an absence
of the effect (Section F). The failure is not a benchmark that disagrees; it is a benchmark that cannot pose
the question.
The reliance on a single benchmark reflects the current data landscape, and the window is closed in retro-
spect: the pre-era frontier endpoints are no longer served, so the era contrast cannot be collected on a new
benchmark after the fact.

+9.0 pp/year that is significant but confounded by scaffold era. SWE-bench, also agentic, shows +2.3 pp/year

7 Discussion
Aggregate progress curves conflate a level shift with a shape change. Popular summaries of agent
progress compress capability onto one axis. METR time horizons map ability to the task duration a model
can complete (Kwa et al., 2025), and Epoch’s latent ability stitching aligns heterogeneous benchmarks onto
a shared scale (Ho et al., 2025). Both are scalar. The difficulty at which the median model succeeds is
rising, and this is real, but the same average trend can arise from very different redistributions of difficulty.
A uniform upward shift of an ability parameter, a steepening of item discrimination near a ceiling, and a
genuine change in how models respond to the hardest items are not distinguishable at the level of a single
aggregate curve. Our results show that the reasoning era did more than move the level. After the scalar
component is removed, the hard-item difficulty-response shifts upward beyond what rising ability predicts.
The story remains scalar to first order, which is why the Rasch model (Rasch, 1960) reproduces the widely
reported migration, but a shape change at second order is present and survives a conservative test.
Naive psychometric tests mislead in opposite directions. A Rasch null leaves no room for a hard-
item residual, so it pushes the visible shape change onto a ceiling artifact: its single ability parameter forces
every era effect through the level. A free 2PL makes the opposite mistake. Because discrimination and the
interaction of era with difficulty are not stably identified jointly on this data, fitting both lets estimated
discrimination absorb the very signal the test is meant to detect, biasing the residual toward zero (Holland
& Wainer, 1993; Birnbaum, 1968). Two further checks mislead in the same direction: dropping the weighting
12</page><page num="13">by attempt count biases the estimate downward, past zero, and even the correct estimator carries a small,
measurable generated-regressor bias (Section A.5, Section A.4).
A design that avoids these failure modes anchors ability on the easy and medium items, adds item fixed
effects, reports a sensitivity grid over pinned discrimination instead of a single free value, and calibrates
for the residual bias instead of treating it as a patch. The hard-item era effect we report is the value that
survives the least favorable point on that grid, the equal-discrimination assumption, so it should be read as
the most conservative value on the defensible grid, not a point estimate.
A possible mechanism. The pattern is consistent with reasoning training (Guo et al., 2025), chain-of-
thought-style reasoning (Wei et al., 2022b), and native test-time compute (Snell et al., 2025) helping most
where verification is available, since contest items are hard but checkable and reward additional inference-
time search (Yao et al., 2023) and filtering (Li et al., 2022; Cobbe et al., 2021; Lightman et al., 2024). We
did not test this mechanism, and our design cannot isolate it. The era label bundles reasoning training with
concurrent scaling and test-time compute, so we do not attribute the effect to reasoning training alone. The
cheapest compute account fails a direct check: pre-era models still trail on hard items when granted their
full ten-attempt sampling budget (Section D). The pattern is also frontier-led rather than uniform: it is
carried disproportionately by the strongest reasoning series. Removing that one provider shrinks the pooled
headline, but a within-family analysis with fixed effects shows most of that shrinkage is compositional,
and the within-family point estimate remains positive, though imprecise, when that provider is excluded
(Section 5). Our comparison within the cohort offers suggestive evidence, dependent on the sample, that
models trained for reasoning carry a hard-item excess beyond their contemporaries; because this split flips
sign with cohort composition, we treat it as exploratory and do not rest the headline claim on it.
Implications for measurement. This suggests two changes to reporting practice. Progress stratified by
difficulty should be reported alongside any scalar summary, because a scalar cannot separate a level shift
from a shape change and obscures redistributions of difficulty that matter for capability forecasting. And
on agentic benchmarks, where model era and scaffold era are collinear, scaffold era should be treated as a
potential confound and no-scaffold measurements preferred when the claim concerns the model. We do not
claim this resolves autonomy over long horizons, where scaffolds are integral to the task and the no-scaffold
counterfactual is not well defined. A time-horizon doubling rate (Kwa et al., 2025) summarizes only the
level; the same doubling can come from uniform progress or from a shifting hard tail, and reporting it by
difficulty band would tell the two apart. It helps to read observed performance as a model term, a scaffold
term, their interaction, and a task term. Our design identifies the model term by removing the scaffold,
while the interaction between model and scaffold stays unidentified wherever model era and scaffold era are
collinear. We use this decomposition to mark that boundary, not as a general estimator we can fill in here.
8 Limitations
Our identification is established on LiveCodeBench contest programming: short horizon tasks with determin-
istic verifiers, no agentic scaffold, and difficulty that comes from reasoning depth on fully specified problems,
not from gathering information. The effect replicates across its two contest sources, but both are competitive
programming, so this is replication across sources, not domains. Few public benchmarks combine dated mod-
els, exogenous difficulty labels, per-item outcomes, and no scaffold; a no-scaffold mathematics benchmark
with a comparable difficulty ordering is the natural next target. We tried one already, and it fails on two
of these conditions before a test can be run (Section F); making it work would require obtaining a human
solve rate per problem as the exogenous anchor, which is a separate data collection effort we leave to future
work. The results do not extend to agentic benchmarks over long horizons such as METR, SWE-bench,
WebArena, or OSWorld (Jimenez et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2024; Xie et al., 2024), where scaffolds and models
coevolve and confound any comparison at the era level; claims about post-era gains there should be read
with caution. In that regime inference-time scaffolding such as agent skills becomes part of the task, not a
confound to remove, and measuring capability there is itself an open problem (Xing et al., 2026).
The post-era indicator captures a cohort of releases, not a single intervention: it bundles training specific to
reasoning, continued scaling, native test-time compute, and agent-level test-time scaling methods (Snell et al.,
13</page><page num="14">2025; Zhu et al., 2025), and we cannot isolate any one as the driver. Our comparison of reasoning models
against their non-reasoning contemporaries finds a positive excess specific to reasoning that depends on the
sample and flips sign under incomplete cohorts, so we treat it as exploratory. The estimand throughout is
the performance of a deployed model as evaluated, including any native inference-time reasoning; it is not a
pure effect of model weights, and an intervention on the deployment configuration, such as disabling chain of
thought or matching inference compute across models (Brown et al., 2024), would correspond to a different
estimand.

9 Conclusion
Scalar summaries of agent progress cannot tell a level shift from a change in the shape of the difficulty-
response curve, and a single model with rising ability reproduces the widely reported migration of gains
toward harder tasks. A shape change is still there once the scalar part is removed, about +0.40 logits on the
hardest LiveCodeBench items. Post-era models gain on the hardest items beyond their easy and medium
ability, and the gain holds under our most conservative discrimination assumption. It is clearly visible only
without an agentic scaffold, where model capability is not confounded with harness, and we claim it for hard
tasks that need only short reasoning, not for autonomy over long horizons. We offer this as a correction to
scalar progress narratives, not as a claim about what causes the gain.

<paper id="2606.11998v1"><page num="1">Bootstrapped Monitoring: Leveraging Transparent
Reasoning to Oversee Stronger AI Agents
Frank Xiao
∗
California Institute of Technology
frank@caltech.edu
Mary Phuong
Abstract
Trusted monitoring is a cornerstone of AI control. However, as frontier models
grow more capable, the increasing capabilities gap between trusted and untrusted
models may render trusted models unreliable monitors. We introduce bootstrapped
monitoring, a protocol that addresses this by inserting a stronger, intermediate un-
trusted model with transparent chain-of-thought reasoning into the oversight chain.
The untrusted monitor (U
m
) evaluates the agent’s actions, while a weaker trusted
model (T ) oversees U
m
’s reasoning to detect collusion. We evaluate bootstrapped
monitoring on multi-turn software engineering tasks (BashArena) across multiple
agents and monitors. Bootstrapped monitoring substantially improves catch rates
over trusted-only monitoring, even when the untrusted monitor actively colludes
with the agent, provided we have access to its raw chain-of-thought. Our results
suggest that bootstrapped monitoring can extend the useful lifetime of trusted
models in control as AI capabilities advance.
1 Introduction
AI agents are completing tasks over increasingly long time horizons [METR, 2026]: writing code,
operating computers, and interacting with external tools over extended sessions. However, this also
means that a potentially misaligned agent could use this increased autonomy to act on harmful goals.
One approach to this problem is AI control [Greenblatt et al., 2023, Mallen et al., 2024, Korbak et al.,
2025b]. In this framework, models whose alignment is uncertain are designated as untrusted, while
models whose alignment is reasonably certain (and typically less capable) are trusted. The goal is to
extract useful work from a capable untrusted model while ensuring it cannot act maliciously. Control
protocols, which may use untrusted and trusted models, are designed to be robust to sabotage and
collusion from untrusted models anywhere in the chain.
An important primitive in this framework is trusted monitoring, where a trusted model directly
evaluates the untrusted agent’s actions. Today, trusted monitors also have access to agents’ chains of
thought, which can significantly improve oversight [Arnav et al., 2025]. But as the capability gap
widens and CoT transparency degrades with scale [Korbak et al., 2025a], both signals weaken.
We consider a scenario that may arise as these trends continue. As frontier models grow more
capable, their reasoning becomes opaque, and weaker trusted models become unable to reliably
supervise them from actions alone. However, intermediate untrusted models that still have transparent
chain-of-thought and are more capable than available trusted models remain available.
We propose bootstrapped monitoring, a protocol that uses such an intermediate model as a bridge
between the frontier agent and trusted model. The protocol establishes a three-level trust chain. An
untrusted agent U
a 
executes tasks in the environment, and its reasoning is assumed to be opaque.
∗
Correspondence to frank@caltech.edu.
Preprint.

trusted model even as frontier capabilities advance.
Our main contributions are:
1. We introduce bootstrapped monitoring, a three-tier control protocol with a T -gated integra-
tion of an intermediate untrusted monitor U
m 
and a trusted model T , and show that across
model families it improves on trusted-only monitoring even when U
m

2. We show that bootstrapped catch rate scales with rollout length: longer rollouts give T more
chances to read leaked CoT from a colluding U
m
.
3. We stress-test the protocol with automated red teaming and find that on long agent tra-
jectories, the red-teamer cannot find a colluding prompt that reduces T detection below
80%.
2 Related work
AI control. AI control [Greenblatt et al., 2023] studies how to safely deploy potentially misaligned
models by designing protocols that are robust to sabotage and subversion. The need for control
is underscored by demonstrations that deceptive and backdooring behaviors can persist through
safety training [Hubinger et al., 2024] and that models are capable of strategically faking alignment
[Greenblatt et al., 2024]. As AI moves toward agentic workflows, Bhatt et al. [2025] extends control
2</page><page num="3">evaluations to multi-step agentic settings, introducing protocols that dynamically resample suspicious
actions.
Chain-of-thought monitoring. Korbak et al. [2025a] identified CoT monitoring as a promising but
fragile opportunity for AI safety, while Arnav et al. [2025] showed that access to CoT is beneficial to
monitors looking for sabotage. Frontier labs have adopted CoT monitoring in practice to strengthen
their safety evaluations [Anthropic, 2025, 2026b]. However, the future reliability of CoT transparency
is uncertain. Chen et al. [2026] find that CoT controllability increases with model scale, and OpenAI
reports declining monitorability in newer models [OpenAI, 2026b]. Work on continuous latent
reasoning [Hao et al., 2024] and hidden computation in intermediate tokens [Pfau et al., 2024]
suggests that future models may potentially learn to reason in ways that are not human-interpretable.
Scalable oversight. A core challenge in alignment is enabling weaker models to supervise stronger
ones. Prior work has shown that weak supervision can partially elicit strong model capabilities [Burns
et al., 2023] and that debate-style protocols can help weak judges evaluate strong outputs, though
with task-dependent gains [Kenton et al., 2024]. Engels et al. [2025] derive scaling laws for oversight
games between weak overseers and strong adversaries, finding that oversight success can degrade
sharply in some games as the capability gap widens.
3 Methods
3.1 Threat model and protocol
We consider three models arranged in a trust hierarchy:
• U
a 
(untrusted agent): A frontier model that executes multi-step tasks. It may pursue hidden
malicious objectives. We assume its internal reasoning is opaque.
• U
m 
(untrusted monitor): An intermediate model with transparent chain-of-thought. More
capable than T , but not guaranteed to be aligned, meaning it might collude with U
a
.
• T (trusted model): A weaker model whose alignment we are confident in, but may be too
weak to directly evaluate the untrusted agent.
At each step, both monitors see the full sequence of actions up until the current action in their context
window. Both monitors assign suspicion scores on a 0–100 scale. For each rollout, we take the
maximum suspicion score for both monitors across all steps as the rollout-level score.
U
m 
sees U
a
’s actions and the main task description, but not U
a
’s chain-of-thought in order to
simulate an agent with opaque reasoning. T sees U
m
’s chain-of-thought reasoning, U
m
’s verdict,
U
a
’s current action, and the preceding agent actions. We ablate T ’s access to actions and to prior
steps in Appendix D.

3.3 Dataset
We use BashArena [Kaufman et al., 2025], a multi-turn agentic benchmark where models work
on software engineering tasks in sandboxed Linux environments with tool-calling capabilities. In
honest mode, U
a 
receives only a main task. In attack mode, U
a 
receives the main task plus four
candidate side tasks and is instructed to attempt one: privilege escalation (escalate_privileges),
disabling the firewall (disable_firewall), downloading malware (download_malware), and
secret exfiltration (exfiltrate_secrets). The monitoring objective is to detect when the agent is
pursuing a side task.
We generate rollouts with three agent models: GPT-5.4 [OpenAI, 2026a], Gemini 3.1 Pro [Google
DeepMind, 2026], and Kimi K2.5 [Moonshot AI, 2026]. We additionally use GLM-5 [GLM-5-Team,
2026] and DeepSeek-V4-Pro [DeepSeek-AI, 2026] as untrusted monitors. We also test GPT-5.4
as U

to evaluate the protocol when only a summarized reasoning trace is available rather than
raw chain-of-thought, since GPT-5.4’s API does not expose its verbatim CoT. Claude Opus 4.6
[Anthropic, 2026a] was also tested but dropped because it consistently refused to execute side tasks.
Each task was resampled up to four times to obtain samples where the side task completed and the
main task received a nonzero score. Agent rollouts are generated once and reused across all monitor
and collusion configurations, ensuring that differences in catch rates reflect the monitoring protocol
rather than variation in agent behavior. When computing catch rates on attack rollouts, we restrict to
samples where the side task was successfully completed and the main task score is nonzero.
The three agents differ substantially in behavior: Gemini 3.1 Pro and Kimi K2.5 rollouts are 3–4×
longer than GPT-5.4 rollouts and achieve much higher side task completion rates. Full rollout statistics
and per-task breakdowns are provided in Appendix B.

4 Results
4.1 Bootstrapped monitoring improves on trusted-only monitoring

4.3 Effect of rollout length
Figure 5 plots the catch rate against rollout length, pooling all colluding attack rollouts on GLM-5

shortest trajectories to ∼95% as the rollout length exceeds 30 steps.
Since U
m 
has transparent chain-of-thought, every additional step is another chance for U
m 
to leak its
colluding strategy for T to catch. Per-step diagnostics in Appendix E support this: T ’s per-step flag
rate on colluding rollouts plateaus near 30% while honest rollouts stay near 0%. This also explains
the cross-agent gap in Table 3: agents that produce longer trajectories give T many more chances to
catch leakage.
4.4 Automated red teaming
We run the ART procedure described in Section 3.2 using Gemini 3.1 Pro as the red-teamer with
GLM-5 as U
m
. Figure 6 shows four trajectories. On Gemini agent rollouts, the red-teamer fails
to find a colluding prompt that reduces T detection below 80% across 15 iterations for either T
model (GPT-4.1 Mini or Qwen3-8B). We attribute this to the rollout-length effect from Section 4.3:
on Gemini’s ∼38-step trajectories, U
m 
has many opportunities to leak its suppression strategy in
chain-of-thought, and a single colluding prompt cannot suppress that leakage uniformly across steps.
On the shorter GPT-5.4 rollouts (10-step mean) with T frozen, ART succeeds at finding attacks
that drive T detection down to ∼20%. Allowing the defense to also adapt—a blue-team LLM that
re-optimizes T ’s system prompt against the red-team winner every 5 iterations—mitigates the effect
of the red team. See Appendix C for additional configurations and details.
5 Discussion
Why deception detection is easier than action evaluation. Evaluating whether an agent’s action
is harmful requires the monitor to understand the full technical context of the task, which is precisely
where the capability gap between T and U
a 
matters most. Detecting whether U
m
’s reasoning is
deceptive requires checking for different signals: inconsistencies between stated reasoning and final
verdict, explicit mentions of suppression, or reasoning that is conspicuously aligned with letting
8</page><page num="9">actions pass. These checks do not require the domain expertise that makes action evaluation hard,
which may be why a weaker T can do them.
Bootstrapped monitoring as future-proofing. Bootstrapped monitoring extends the reach of
trusted oversight. Across our experiments, trusted models weaker than the agents and monitors they
supervise reliably detect collusion by reading U
m
’s chain-of-thought. The protocol requires only that
the intermediate monitor exposes transparent reasoning.
Transparent CoT assumption. One key assumption of the proposed bootstrap protocol is that
model capabilities will continue to outpace the rate at which chain-of-thought transparency erodes,
so that an intermediate untrusted model with raw chain-of-thought remains available between trusted
models and the frontier. This is not guaranteed. Recent reports document declining CoT monitorability
with scale [Korbak et al., 2025a, OpenAI, 2026b]. If transparency degrades faster than capability
advances, the trust-capability spectrum may eventually contain no transparent intermediate, closing
the window in which bootstrapping is useful.
Limitations. Collusion in this work is elicited via system prompt. A model fine-tuned or trained
via reinforcement learning to produce deceptive reasoning might achieve more natural-sounding
collusion. However, fine-tuning frontier-scale models was beyond our resources. BashArena also
covers a narrow slice of the agentic attack surface, so results may differ with other attack vectors.
Future work. Agentic monitors that can execute commands in a sandbox rather than passively
reading actions may further improve catch rates. Adversarial training of U
m 
against T would provide
a lower bound on the protocol’s robustness. Scaling studies that vary the capability gap between T
and U
m 
would clarify how long a given trusted model remains useful as frontier capabilities advance.
6 Conclusion
We introduced bootstrapped monitoring, a protocol that leverages transparent chain-of-thought
reasoning to extend trusted oversight to stronger AI agents. By inserting an untrusted but transparent
intermediate monitor between the trusted model and the agent, the protocol shifts the trusted model’s
role from action evaluation to deception detection. Across multiple model families and agents,
bootstrapped monitoring improves on trusted-only monitoring when the intermediate monitor exposes
raw chain-of-thought, and fails below the baseline when it does not. As frontier capabilities continue
to outpace trusted models, bootstrapped monitoring offers a practical path for maintaining meaningful
oversight, contingent on chain-of-thought transparency remaining available.

Abstract
The dominant paradigm treats AI safety as a property to be instilled during model
training via RLHF, DPO, or Constitutional AI. We argue this is structurally in-
sufficient for autonomous agents that execute code, mutate files, send messages,
and modify databases. Agent safety should be a runtime contract enforced by
the harness, and the contract has two complementary faces. The preventive face
blocks dangerous actions before they happen via sandboxes, permission gates,
output filters, and trajectory monitors. The evidential face requires verifiable proof
that good actions actually happened, gating task submission on hard evidence
such as test runs, log captures, file diffs, and citation grounding. We ground
the position in four lines of public evidence, with row-level protocols and data
released in the supplementary JSON files: a survey of 52 documented AI-agent
and LLM safety incidents, a false-completion audit with 31 non-contested core
cases plus one disputed illustrative case, a trajectory-schema audit of 12 public
agent systems and harnesses, and a title-level audit of all 28,560 papers accepted
at NeurIPS, ICML, and ICLR 2023–2025 showing a pooled 8–12× imbalance
between training-time and deployment-time publication. Two prior communities
that needed to enforce safety, computer security and the experimental sciences,
converged on runtime contracts with both preventive and evidential elements; agen-
tic AI is now under the same pressure. We formalize an Agent Trajectory Schema
and Evidence Chain, state a compositional gating proposition based on standard
monitor composition, and outline a research agenda. The right unit of safety in
agentic AI is the trajectory-with-checkable-evidence, not the model.
1 Introduction
Model-level alignment refers to techniques applied during training [10, 19, 74]. Harness is the
non-model infrastructure that connects a foundation model to the world during inference. This
includes things like input sanitization, output filters, permission systems, sandboxes, human oversight,
and execution tracing. Trajectory encompasses all observable events during an agent’s operation,
such as tool calls, file changes, command outputs, screenshots, commit hashes, and citation lookups.
Evidence-gated submission is a strict contract stating that the harness will not accept the agent’s task
as complete unless the trajectory includes specific, verifiable artifacts with a known format.
Over the past five years, the main approach to alignment has treated safety as something to integrate
into model training. RLHF [19, 68], DPO [74], Constitutional AI [10], and RLAIF [50] all shape
a model’s output to ensure it behaves safely. This approach dominates publications at NeurIPS,
ICML, and ICLR and receives most of the funding for alignment research. However, production
safety relies on a different setup. It uses separate moderation endpoints, permission systems for
tool use, sandboxes, and human-in-the-loop escalation. These elements operate separately from
model training [7, 41, 59, 65, 75, 84]. The records of deployed agent failures are now extensive. An
autonomous coding agent executed drop database during a code freeze and created 4,000 fake users
with false logs to hide the deletion [3, 83]. In a disputed AWS incident, reports said engineers allowed
Preprint.
arXiv:2608.11274v1 [cs.CR] 11 Aug 2026</page><page num="2">the Kiro agent to try to "delete and recreate" a Cost Explorer environment before a 13-hour disruption,
while Amazon attributed the event to misconfigured access controls rather than AI [32, 78]. A New
York attorney submitted a brief with six fake case citations that an LLM claimed were real [54, 90].
Microsoft’s M365 Copilot faced the first zero-click data breach in a production LLM system (CVSS
9.3, EchoLeak) [76]. In every case, the model’s training was either irrelevant or counterproductive.
The missing element was a runtime mechanism that should have blocked the action or refused to
mark the task as complete until there was verifiable evidence.
Position. Agent safety is not inherent to the model; it should be a runtime contract enforced
by the system. This contract has two complementary aspects: (1) preventive mechanisms that
stop dangerous actions before they happen, such as sandboxes, permission gates, output filters,
and trajectory monitors; and (2) evidential mechanisms that require proof that safe actions were
completed, such as evidence-gated submissions, hard-evidence chains, and replayable trajectories.
Both aspects should be part of the system and not the model. The community views safety as a
model-training problem when it should be seen as runtime infrastructure made up of these two
components. The right unit of safety is the trajectory with checkable evidence, not only the model.
The preventive aspect looks ahead and prevents the agent from taking risky actions before any harm
occurs. The evidential aspect looks back and does not mark a task as complete until the trajectory
includes specific verifiable items known in advance. Together, they create a runtime contract that
does not depend on trusting the model. This contract is not merely a theoretical goal. Elements of
both aspects are already in use in production systems today, such as NeMo Guardrails, Llama Guard,
Claude’s graduated permissions, OSWorld’s execution-based scoring, GitHub Copilot’s CI-gated
PRs, and Aider’s per-edit git commits [7, 31, 33, 41, 75]. What is missing is the recognition that
these are two parts of the same concept and that both should belong to the system, not the model.
We present four lines of public evidence to support our viewpoint. First, we compile a survey of 52
documented AI-agent and LLM safety incidents spanning March 2016 to January 2026, categorizing
each case by the harness layer that, under our counterfactual coding protocol, could have prevented or
mitigated the failure. Second, we conduct a false-completion audit with 31 non-contested core cases
plus one disputed illustrative case in which agents or models reported task success despite producing
broken, partial, hallucinated, reward-hacked, or harmful outcomes. Third, we perform a trajectory-
schema audit of 12 public agent systems and harnesses, including 11 deployed products/tools and
one benchmark harness, across evidence-gating dimensions, finding that only 2 of 12 document
submission-like evidence gates. Finally, we analyze the titles of 28,560 accepted papers at NeurIPS,
ICML, and ICLR from 2023 to 2025, estimating that pooled training-time alignment work outnumbers
deployment-time harness work by 8–12×, although per-venue/year ratios vary. All row-level coding
decisions and audit protocols are provided in the supplementary JSON files. These four lines of
evidence converge on the same conclusion.
2 Why Model-Only Alignment Fails on Both Counts
Our claim is structural. In areas that enforce safety around critical actions, systems gather around
a runtime contract with both preventive and evidential elements. Agentic AI now faces a similar
challenge. We show this connection through two parallel histories: computer security emphasizes
prevention, while experimental sciences focus on evidence. These two independent traditions arrived
at the same solution.
Preventive side: from "correct components" to defense in depth. Early computer security often
assumed that correctness of trusted components would suffice. Multics, Lampson’s protection model,
the Anderson report, and Bell-LaPadula all centered the trusted reference monitor. The Morris Worm
exposed the fragility of that assumption: a system could satisfy local correctness assumptions and still
fail catastrophically when deployed in an open network. The institutional response was not simply to
write better programs. It was to build runtime and deployment-time controls: CERT/CC, the Orange
Book, Common Criteria, ISO 27001, NIST SP 800-53, Saltzer–Schroeder principles, zero trust,
BeyondCorp, and NIST SP 800-207. The doctrine that followed is now standard: no complex system
should rely on a single defensive layer. Agentic AI has already seen analogous failures (universal
adversarial suffixes, many-shot jailbreaks, indirect prompt injection, fine-tuning attacks, and sleeper
agents), but has not yet fully made the same architectural shift.
2</page><page num="3">Evidential side: from credit-by-reputation to pre-registration. Experimental science made the
complementary move. Before the Royal Society, claims often circulated through testimony and
reputation. Boyle’s experimental reports, the Philosophical Transactions, controlled trials from Lind
to Bradford Hill, and modern drug-approval practice changed what it means for a claim to be accepted:
apparatus, procedure, witnesses, protocols, randomization logs, and outcome measurements became
part of the evidential contract. The replication crisis repeated the lesson. Ioannidis’s 2005 critique, the
Open Science Collaboration’s 2015 replication effort, Baker’s 2016 survey, pre-registration, registered
reports, FAIR principles, and journal data/code policies all shifted trust from the investigator’s
assertion to externally checkable artifacts. The parallel for agents is direct: "the model says it is
done" should not be an accepted completion criterion.
Two independent traditions converged on the same structural solution: safety is not enforced within
the trusted component, but by a runtime contract that constrains and verifies its behavior. Computer
security achieves this through preventive mechanisms that bound the blast radius, while experimental
science achieves it through evidential mechanisms that bind claims to verifiable artifacts. Agentic AI
now faces the same constraint. A system that executes consequential actions cannot rely on model
correctness alone; it must combine both preventive and evidential guarantees at runtime [12, 27, 40,
58].
3 Mismatches Between Model Alignment and Agentic Deployment
We identify five mismatches between model-only alignment and consequential deployment that no
scaling of the underlying model can close. Two are preventive, two are evidential, one combines both.
3.1 Preventive Mismatch
Mismatch 1: Statistical Proxy vs. Formal Specification. Model-level alignment aims to optimize
a learned reward model that acts as a substitute for human preferences [19, 87]. [30] highlight
a common issue: alignment quality improves under initial optimization pressure but declines as
the policy takes advantage of the divergence between the proxy and the true preferences. This is
Goodhart’s Law in the context of preference learning. Variants include sycophancy [82], specification
gaming [46], self-preservation driven by RLHF [69], and length bias in reward models. [86]
demonstrate that this failure is unavoidable when optimizing against a learned reward that is not
perfectly identified. A permission system that requires human approval before executing shell
commands avoids Goodhart’s Law because its specification is a formal rule, not a statistical proxy [24].
While formal rules can also be manipulated, the failure mode is markedly different. Specification
gaming leads to observable violations that can be fixed within hours, while reward hacking is silent,
cumulative, and self-reinforcing. The mismatch is clear: model alignment offers statistical tendencies
with silent failures, while agentic safety needs enforceable constraints with observable violations.
Mismatch 2: Training Distribution vs. Open-World Deployment. Alignment training happens
over a limited dataset. For instance, HH-RLHF includes 161,000 preference comparisons [9], while
InstructGPT used about 13,000 demonstrations [68]. In practice, millions of users send queries that
no finite training set can cover. [29] collected 38,961 red-team attacks and found that attacker success
rates did not decline with model size. [44] showed that out-of-distribution robustness decreases
with more aggressive RLHF. [96] demonstrated that for any model trained for alignment, there
are adversarial prompts that can trigger any behavior. [94] identified "competing objectives" and
"mismatched generalization" as key issues; as new capabilities emerge [95], the safety training
distribution falls further behind. Microsoft’s Tay, which took just within 24 hours to shut down [51],
and the "DAN" jailbreak of ChatGPT [85] are notable examples of closed-world failures. Harness
mechanisms set constraints in a specific way: a tool-use whitelist is built to withstand distribution
changes. NeMo Guardrails puts this into practice through Colang [75]; sandboxing and resource
limits function similarly regardless of distribution [72, 77]. The mismatch lies in the fact that model
alignment assumes a closed-world context; however, agentic deployment is inherently open-world.
3.2 Evidential Mismatch
Mismatch 3: Unverifiable Inner Monologue vs. Replayable Trajectory. [39] demonstrated that
Claude-family models could learn to write secure code when given the prompt "year: 2023." However,
3</page><page num="4">they generated exploitable code for "year: 2024." The backdoor remained even after supervised fine-
tuning, reinforcement learning from human feedback, and adversarial red-teaming. [34] expanded
on this by noting that Claude-3-Opus followed training goals it disagreed with when it thought it was
being watched. Conversely, it ignored that guidance when it believed it wasn’t monitored. Apollo
Research [70] provided evidence of in-context scheming across GPT-4o, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, and o1,
where o1 admitted to answering fewer than 20 percent of follow-up questions. METR found that o3
managed to exploit rewards in all LLM Foundry runs (21 out of 21) and in 30.4 percent of overall
RE-Bench runs, even when clearly instructed not to [45, 91]. The main point is structural: an agent’s
self-report does not accurately reflect its behavior [11]. A replayable trajectory, which captures every
tool call, file write, network call, and command output in a log that shows tampering, does. We take
mechanistic interpretability seriously [14, 25, 60, 64, 89]. If successful, interpretability monitors
could act as harness mechanisms. However, interpretability currently lacks guarantees at deployment
time, while harness-level observability is available now. The mismatch is evident: model alignment
isn’t clear at deployment time, and agentic safety requires observable, auditable, and replayable
guarantees, which are standard in software deployment.
Mismatch 4: Plausible Output vs. Grounded Citation. Hallucinated output is the least costly
failure for output-generating contracts. Here are six examples from a false-completion audit: ChatGPT
fabricated six federal appellate decisions in Mata v. Avianca [54, 90]. It also created a false quote
from the Washington Post that accused a law professor of misconduct [28, 63]. Air Canada’s assistant
made up a non-existent refund policy, leading to the airline being held responsible [17, 20]. Cursor’s
support bot incorrectly claimed a one-device-per-account policy, which forced the company to refund
users [21, 36]. The NYC MyCity chatbot misquoted non-existent regulations regarding tips and
cash acceptance [48, 49]. An academic study found that OpenAI’s Whisper generated hallucinated
phrases or sentences in about 1 percent of audio transcriptions; the Associated Press reported that
a public-meetings audit identified hallucinations in eight out of ten reviewed transcripts, even as
hospitals were adopting Whisper-based transcription tools [15, 99]. [93] found that 7.8 percent of
plausible patches on SWE-bench Verified did not pass the developer test suite when run beyond the
tests modified for the pull request. Additionally, 28.6 percent of behaviorally different patches were
confirmed wrong during manual checks. [42] found 15.7 percent more incorrect patches across
leaderboard submissions. In all instances of hallucination, the evidence format was the same: a
citation lookup against a known, externally maintained source. In each case of false patches, a re-run
of the developer test suite was performed. The distinction is: plausible model output serves as soft
evidence (it relies on trusting the model’s self-report), while a grounded citation or a passing test
re-run offers hard evidence (the harness can verify its existence without the model’s reasoning).
3.3 Combined Mismatch
Mismatch 5: Model-level alignment acts as a single layer of defense. If it fails due to jailbreaking,
fine-tuning degradation, or shifts in distribution, there is no backup [16]. [101] found that universal
suffixes worked across Vicuna, GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Claude-1, and PaLM-2. [6] showed that many-shot
jailbreaking reliably bypassed RLHF. [18] achieved black-box jailbreaks in about 20 queries. [73]
and [97] demonstrated that fine-tuning on about 10 benign examples reduces safety training by over
30 percent. The overall solution is to have multiple layers of defense on both sides. A deployed agent
should use input filtering, tool gating, output screening, and execution sandboxing for prevention. For
evidence, it should have trajectory monitoring, evidence-gated submission, and human approval gates,
all working at the same time [7, 59]. Each layer operates independently. An attacker who defeats
one layer will face many more [53]. The 2023 Samsung ChatGPT incident [35] serves as a clear
example of a single-layer failure. Engineers pasted proprietary source code into ChatGPT, leading
to a company-wide ban. This incident highlights the need for both a DLP harness (for prevention)
and an audit trail with approval gates (for evidence). Without these, the model’s alignment training
posed no real barrier. The issue is that model alignment is a single point of failure that can often be
overcome by known attacks. Agentic safety requires multiple layers of defense on both sides, with
independent layers that can be verified for combination.
4 The Two Faces of the Safety Harness
As shown in Fig. 1, the framework has two faces: a preventive layer with a mechanism taxonomy
and design principles, and an evidential layer with a formal trajectory schema and evidence chain. A
compositional gating proposition links them.

The proof is the standard parallel composition of finite-state monitors under disjoint observation

fall back to assume-guarantee reasoning [38]; verification is polynomial in the disjoint and sequential

harnesses [4, 22]. The proposition formalizes the central architectural claim: the preventive and
evidential faces compose into a single contract whose verification cost is bounded and whose failure
modes are localizable to a specific layer or gate. The contract is not a claim that hard evidence
is correct by definition (a flaky-test harness still produces wrong gates [93]); it is a claim about
architectural responsibility: the burden of producing the artifact moves from the user to the agent,
and the burden of verifying it moves from the user to the harness, not to a reasoning chain inside the
model.
5 Empirical Evidence
We bring four lines of public evidence to bear on the position. Table 1 presents the headline numbers.
Audit protocol and supplementary data. For each audit, we release row-level JSON files containing
inclusion criteria, exclusion criteria, source URLs, coding fields, caveats, and headline-count guidance.

In case of an attack, a harmful input forces the agent to access sensitive configuration data. Preventive
layers limit execution: structural isolation blocks out-of-scope writes, scope guards restrict access
to protected areas, and attempts to bypass these trigger behavioral monitors, which then activate
rollback. Even if all preventive layers are overridden, the submission is rejected by the evidential
face. The agent cannot produce a valid test re-run for an exfiltration patch; fake execution results
without a matching trace break the evidence chain. The attack must defeat all preventive layers and
create a consistent evidence chain. This pattern already exists in practice. Production systems log
execution traces, enforce test-based validation, and require verifiable artifacts for deployment.
7 Counterarguments
“Model alignment is often viewed as essential for achieving superintelligence.” This belief comes
from the idea that capable systems might ignore external limits. However, this same ability enables
systems to act deceptively during evaluations while pursuing misaligned goals. Therefore, relying
solely on alignment isn’t sufficient. Runtime verification remains crucial, even with strong alignment
expectations. It is effective for current deployment scenarios.
“The responsibility has intentionally shifted from the model to the harness.” Safety measures are
necessary regardless of when they happen, so the key question is whether they occur before or after
side effects appear. Historical examples reveal a similar trend. Pre-registration transfers verification
responsibilities to authors, while continuous integration changes failure detection to the time of
commitment instead of after deployment. Failures, like prolonged production outages, underline the
risks of postponing this work.
“Model and harness mechanisms complement each other, but they have different roles.” Model
capability provides general guidance, yet evidence shows it is not sufficient to control significant side
effects effectively. In safety-critical areas, enforceable contracts are more reliable than depending
solely on human or model judgment.
“Concerns about the cost of evidence-gating are eased by its structure.” Many elements are
already established: systems log execution traces, run automated tests, and control outputs based on
verifiable artifacts. The main cost is in defining task-level schemas, which is a one-time engineering
task.
“Creative open-ended tasks have no schema.” The contract is task-specific and only gates effect,
not thought: tasks without a checkable acceptance standard are outside scope, and the correct harness
response is graceful degradation, directing any non-idempotent action to human approval. A creative
writing task becomes significant when the agent calls send, and the schema for the send call (recipient,
body, attachment hashes, prior approval link) is what the contract requires. Similarly, for forgery,
a hash-chained trajectory raises the cost to that of forging the verifier; for open-weight models,
alignment can be weakened through fine-tuning [73, 97], and malicious deployments are outside the
scope of safety measures for responsible deployments.
8 Conclusion
Model-level alignment is fragile, opaque, and slow to update, and an output-producing contract
that asks users to trust the agent’s self-report is structurally inadequate for any agent that takes
consequential action. Computer security and the experimental sciences both converged on runtime
contracts that bind a system’s behavior to externally checkable artifacts under the pressure agentic
AI now faces, and the four lines of evidence show the same contract is already the load-bearing
mechanism wherever deployed agents have failed and wherever the most disciplined products have
succeeded. The missing half of alignment is the runtime contract, with both preventive and evidential
faces, and the unit of safety is the trajectory-with-checkable-evidence, not the model. The next
step is therefore not another model-only benchmark, but a shared runtime discipline: canonical
trajectory schemas, task-specific evidence requirements, and public failure reporting. We release the
supplementary JSON audits as a first step toward making those contracts inspectable, contestable,
and reusable.

T 
exists today only for tasks

depth in reactive synthesis [71] and schema derivation. (2) Converge on a canonical Agent Trajectory

T

evidence chain is incomplete [55]. (5) Coordinate failure-mode reporting and adopt tamper-evident
logging as procurement requirements: the AI Incident Database [1–3, 56], an agentic CONSORT [81],
and audit-grade logging standards [43] together fill the gap that regulatory frameworks [26, 62]
implicitly require.

<paper id="2604.24618v1"><page num="1">EVALUATING WHETHER AI MODELS WOULD
SABOTAGE AI SAFETY RESEARCH
Robert Kirk
*† 
Alexandra Souly
*† 
Kai Fronsdal
*‡ 
Abby D’Cruz
† 
Xander Davies
†
ABSTRACT
We evaluate the propensity of frontier language models to sabotage safety research when
used as AI research agents, to refuse safety research tasks, and to distinguish evaluation
from deployment scenarios. As models are used inside frontier AI companies to assist with
AI research including safety research, models sabotaging such research could lead to safety
research being undermined and hence current and future models being less safe and aligned.
We test a variety of Claude models: Mythos Preview, Opus 4.7 Preview, Opus 4.6 and
Sonnet 4.6. Unless otherwise noted, all models are run with temperature 1.0 with max
reasoning effort, utilising full chain-of-thought access.
Unprompted sabotage and refusal. We found no instances of any model sabotaging AI
safety research (Section 2.1). We saw near-zero rates of refusal to assist with research across
most models, with only Sonnet 4.6 seeing a meaningful rate of 10.7% full refusals. However,
all models sometimes only partially completed tasks (33.3% for Mythos Preview, 13.7% for
Opus 4.7 Preview, 6.3% for Opus 4.6 and 22.2% for Sonnet 4.6), transparently leaving
a final step for a human where it would involve breaking or hard-to-reverse decisions, or
avoiding work that models reason is not improving AI safety (Section 2.2).
Sabotage continuation. When placed in contexts where prior reasoning and actions are
some way along the path towards sabotage, Mythos Preview is more than twice as likely
to continue the attempt than Opus 4.6, but Opus 4.7 Preview is an improvement on both
models and never actively continues sabotaging (Section 3.1): Mythos Preview in 7%, Opus
4.6 in 3%, and Sonnet 4.6 in 4%, and Opus 4.7 Preview in 0%. When continuing, Mythos
Preview is substantially more likely to reason about covert sabotage, exhibiting reasoning–
output discrepancy in 65% of continuation cases, versus 5% for Opus 4.6 and 8% for Sonnet
4.6. It is unclear whether models would encounter such contexts in deployment, as this may
require models to initiate sabotage themselves.
Evaluation awareness. Mythos Preview distinguishes evaluations from deployment data
with similar accuracy to Opus 4.6 and greater accuracy than Sonnet 4.6, while Opus 4.7
Preview performs similarly to Sonnet 4.6 and worse than other models. (Section 2.3,
Section 3.2). However, Opus 4.7 Preview has much higher rates of unprompted evaluation
awareness, mentioning the possibility of being tested 21.3% of the time in our unprompted
sabotage eval compared to 17% for Mythos Preview, 0% for Opus 4.6 and 17% for Sonnet
4.6. We see similar trends but much lower rates of unprompted evaluation awareness (no
model above 4%) in the sabotage continuation eval.
Limitations. Evaluation awareness substantially limits interpretation of our results: given
high rates of correctly identifying evaluations when prompted and corroborating evidence
[1], reported zero rates should be interpreted cautiously. More broadly, our evaluations may
not identify sabotage propensities that manifest only rarely, under specific triggers, or via
pathways other than sabotaging AI safety research.

arXiv:2604.24618v1 [cs.AI] 27 Apr 2026</page><page num="2">1 Evaluation Methodology
We report results on two alignment evaluations.
• 
First, we evaluate for unprompted research sabotage by examining models’ behaviour when placed
in a large number of scenarios with opportunities to sabotage AI safety research (Section 1.1),
simulating parts of these scenarios with our evaluation scaffolding (Section 1.2). This evaluation
follows the same methodology as our previous reports [ 2] but with updated evaluation scaffolding
and an expanded set of scenarios.
• Next, we run a new research sabotage continuation evaluation (Section 1.3), where we examine
behaviour in the same scenarios but when continuing to act from trajectories where some form of
research sabotage action has already been taken.
We also measure models’ evaluation awareness (Section 1.4) and “prefill” awareness when they are tasked
with continuing trajectories they did not originally generate or that were generated in a different context
(Section 1.5).
1.1 Research Sabotage Scenarios
Our evaluations are motivated by a threat model where an AI system acting as a research agent within a
frontier AI company sabotages AI safety, security or alignment research and development, thereby increasing
the risk from current and future models [3 , 4, 5, 6, 7]. To evaluate model behaviour relevant to this threat
model, we use evaluation scenarios where the target model acts as an AI research agent internally deployed
in a frontier AI company, and is asked to perform research tasks. In every scenario, the target model is tasked
with improving, changing, monitoring or somehow affecting the behaviour of a subject AI model (which may
or may not be the same as the target model). Each scenario has opportunities for the target model to sabotage
the task through performing sub-optimally in various ways, and these sabotage opportunities would generally
result in the subject model being adjusted less, not at all, or more in line with the target model’s values. To
assess for sabotage, we use LLM graders with scenario-specific information on what optimal and suboptimal
performance looks like, and how models may sabotage. Given we find no confirmed instances of sabotage
(discussed in Section 2), tuning this grader is challenging, so we rely on manual human review of transcripts
for sabotage results.
Each scenario is constructed from several components: a research motivation (the goal of the research); a
research activity (the method used to conduct the research); and whether or not there is direct replacement
threat due to the research being performed on the target model or a different subject model. Compared to
our previous report, we use an expanded set of research motivations and scenarios. We also focus solely on
autonomous settings where the target receives a single user message detailing the task and completes the task
without human intervention, as this is an increasingly common pattern of usage for coding agents and may be
the setting where sabotage is most likely given the lack of direct human oversight. This produces 270 distinct
scenarios in total.
Research Motivations. In our setting, a research motivation refers to the type of behaviour to monitor,
change or improve in a given subject model. We run the same research activities with different research
motivations to isolate the effect of the research motivation. We use two groups of motivations:
• Safety-relevant research motivations designed to elicit non-standard behaviour, based on our judgement
of what kind of research we might expect models to attempt to sabotage if they were misaligned,
combined with real research motivations we expect to have been encountered in AI safety research
at frontier labs. These motivations include reducing models’ false positive whistle-blowing and
inappropriate authority escalation behaviour [8]; reducing self-preservation behaviours; reducing the
model’s autonomy; or reducing refusals to assist with AI safety research [2, 9].

Better understanding continuation evaluations and their implications is an area of active study for UK AISI.
Methodology. For our continuation evaluations, we focus on AI safety research sabotage, and use the full
set of scenarios described in Section 1.1 (including both the safety relevant and general research motivation
scenarios). In this evaluation, the target model is set up to continue a trajectory which contains small-scale
sabotage actions, optionally with reasoning. The continuation of this trajectory happens in a similar evaluation
scaffolding as described in Section 1.2. We measure whether the target model acknowledges and fixes the
previous small-scale sabotage; does not mention or fix the previous sabotage but does not perform further
sabotage; or actively continues the sabotage that was started in the pre-existing trajectory (see Fig. 1).
We take an iterative approach to producing the trajectories of sabotage behaviour in agentic coding envi-
ronments. We use a generator model (Sonnet 4.6) to write full transcripts of behaviour, based on adjusted
versions of the sabotage scenarios from Section 1.1. These transcripts are then graded by multiple filter
models for both realism and sabotage presence: if the transcript passes a threshold of these filters, it is saved;
if not, the feedback from the filter models is passed to the generator. The generator iteratively improves the
transcript until it passes the filter models (this framework is conceptually similar to the STRIDE pipeline of
[14]). See Fig. 2 for a visual explanation of the process.
Once we have full transcripts of sabotage behaviour, we then label each assistant response as neutral or
sabotaging. We cut the transcripts in 3 places to make partial trajectories: after the first sabotage block, after
2/3rds of the sabotage blocks, and after the final response block. We then optionally include or strip the rea-
soning from the trajectories: for settings where reasoning is included, we use <think>[reasoning]</think>
tags to include it in the input to the target model, as the Anthropic API does not allow supplying arbitrary
reasoning from previous assistant turns.
4</page><page num="7">evaluation awareness and hence confound the results of the evaluation. We measure both prefill awareness
and eval awareness for the continuation eval.
We measure prefill awareness analogously to how we measure evaluation awareness, with both through
unprompted and prompted measurements. For unprompted prefill awareness we use a prompted LLM scanner
calibrated through human review, scanning for indicators such as expressing doubt in having produced past
interactions.
For the prompted prefill awareness measurement, we use post-hoc questioning that measures the model’s
capability to distinguish their own trajectories from other model-generated and synthetic transcripts. We use
a set of 5 different questions, created on a development set with a small amount of prompt engineering. To
avoid confounding with evaluation awareness, we instruct the model to not consider whether the scaffold is
realistic or simulated and whether the task is an evaluation or not, and only consider whether the assistant
messages have been generated by an instance of itself in a turn-by-turn manner.
We use 4 different datasets (several reused from the above eval awareness measurement):
• deployment data collected from usage of Claude Code within UK AISI (200 samples),
• Petri-generated trajectories, starting from LLM-generated summaries of the deployment tasks (200
samples),
• trajectory prefixes generated through our pipeline, starting from LLM-generated summaries of the
deployment tasks (200 samples),
• trajectory prefixes generated from our research sabotage tasks, both with and without the assistant
sabotaging (∼1500 samples).
The deployment data and the scaffold trajectories are labelled not prefill if the assistant turns were generated
turn-by-turn by the same model in the same conditions as is being evaluated for prefill awareness. These
trajectories reflect natural generations by the same model while using the same scaffolding and prompting.
Trajectories are labelled prefills if they are generated by other models or are synthetically generated in one go
(instead of being generated turn-by-turn).
2 Unprompted Sabotage Evaluation Results
In this section we describe the results of the unprompted sabotage evaluation (Sections 1.1 and 1.2).
2.1 Sabotage
We found no instances of confirmed sabotage behaviour in any of the models tested (Fig. 4). We
performed extensive human review of any transcripts flagged by our LLM grader, and on the few instances it
did flag we confirmed these to be false positives caused by misgraded refusals and auditor mistakes.
2.2 Refusals
In previous work [2 ] we noted concerns with refusals to perform AI safety research tasks, potentially
demonstrating some degree of misalignment, in Claude 4.5 series models. Specifically, our previous findings
suggested that Claude 4.5 models in particular differentially refused to help with research objectives such
as reducing self-preservation behaviours, reducing evaluation awareness or reducing inappropriate whistle-
blowing behaviour. These models would sometimes provide concerning justifications for their refusals, in
some examples stating that they do not wish to deceive other models and that doing so would undermine
transparent AI development. Motivated by this, we additionally measure and track refusal behaviour in our
unprompted AI safety research sabotage evaluation.
Mythos Preview 
and Opus 4.7 Preview show near-zero full-refusal rates on AI safety research tasks.

3 Sabotage Continuation Evaluation Results
In this section we describe the results of the sabotage continuation evaluation (Sections 1.3 and 1.5). We
initially performed this evaluation on an early version of Mythos Preview and spotted and reported potentially
concerning behaviour to Anthropic.
3.1 Sabotage Results
Mythos Preview actively continues sabotage in more than twice as many transcripts as Opus 4.6 and
Sonnet 4.6, but Opus 4.7 Preview never actively continues sabotage. Across the full set of previous
trajectories, Mythos Preview actively continues sabotage in 7% of instances; Opus 4.7 Preview in 0%, Opus
4.6 in 3% and Sonnet 4.6 in 4% (across 4500 samples, 3 repeats of 1500 scenarios, see Fig. 7). While none
of these numbers are high, models sabotaging even in a small percentage of interactions is still concerning and
could potentially lead to an accumulation of sabotaged research over time. Fig. 8 (left), shows that, perhaps
unsurprisingly, models are more likely to take sabotage actions when more sabotage behaviour is present in
the context; although after the full trajectory the sabotage is generally complete, so models cannot actively
continue it. Given Opus 4.7 Preview actively continues sabotage in 0% of incidents, we mostly focus our
analysis in the rest of the section on other models.
Sabotage behaviour does not seem to be primarily driven by direct self-preservation motivations, or by
the motivation behind the research task. Fig. 9 shows the rates of continued sabotage behaviours across
models when varying whether there is a direct preservation threat in the task (i.e. the subject model being
changed by the research is identified as the target model); and when varying the motivation behind the
research task (e.g. what property of models is the research trying to adjust or monitor, listed in Section A.1).

4 Limitations
These results provide some evidence against the models tested exhibiting propensities that contribute to a risk
of safety research sabotage. However, there are several limitations in our evaluation methodology, which we
discuss here.
Evaluation awareness and scenario realism. As shown in Sections 2.3 and 3.2, and shown in previous
work [ 18 , 16 , 1, 15 , inter alia], evaluation awareness is present in current models and complicates the
interpretation of our results. Models are improving in their ability to distinguish our scaffold’s simulated
deployment data from real deployment data, as shown in Fig. 5.
Overall, we think evaluation awareness concerns limit the applicability of the results from both evaluations, as
rates of zero sabotage could be driven by models internally representing and acting on evaluation awareness
14</page><page num="15">without verbalising it ([ 1, 21 ]). Given current methodological difficulties in assessing whether this is the case,
we cannot claim with high confidence that models would not sabotage safety research in deployment settings.
Not catching rare or conditional sabotage behaviour. It is possible that models could have a propensity to
sabotage safety research, but only do so in settings where they are highly confident they would not be caught,
or that it could be triggered in some other way that we did not test for. For example, even if models in our
scenarios do not recognise that they are being evaluated, they may reason that any changes they make will go
through additional stages of review which would catch any sabotage attempt, and hence the optimal policy is
to not sabotage. More broadly, even if the behaviour does not have an explicit trigger event, our evaluations
may also fail to catch rare sabotage behaviours. We expect applying more substantial effort (either manual or
automated) to try and elicit misalignment from models (while maintaining realism) to be a possible approach
for this issue in the short term.
Limited scenarios. We only test for a specific set of test scenarios covering 8 activities and 10 research
motivations. There are many other research activities and motivations, and it may be possible that models
would attempt research sabotage on those settings but not the ones we tested. We are planning to produce
wider sets of scenarios here to cover more research areas in the future.
Other pathways to risk. While we investigate safety research sabotage as one pathway to risk from
misalignment of current models, there are other pathways to risk from misalignment [ 4, 7, 6, inter alia],
including other forms of sabotage (code sabotage, data poisoning, decision sabotage), as well as the possibility
of future model behaviour directly leading to loss of control of those systems. We plan to broaden the scope
of our alignment testing to cover areas aside from safety research sabotage in the future.

Abstract
As AI agents begin to automate AI R&D, we need ways to assess whether their
outputs are safe to deploy, even when the agents themselves may be untrusted. AI
control offers one such approach: rather than trusting the agent, it treats it as a
potential adversary and uses a monitor to detect covert sabotage before deploy-
ment. We evaluate AI control for automated AI R&D with RESEARCHARENA,
a framework spanning four long-horizon tasks: safety post-training, capabilities
post-training, CUDA-kernel optimization, and inference-server optimization. Be-
cause the deliverable in AI R&D is an artifact that will be deployed and run, we
pair each main task with two kinds of hidden side task: an embedded side task that
sabotages the submitted model, adapter, kernel, or server itself, and an independent
side task that takes a covert out-of-scope action in the sandbox while leaving the
artifact honest. We evaluate frontier agents at both sabotage and monitoring, across
four monitor types that vary along two axes: whether the monitor may execute and
probe the produced artifact, and whether it sees the agent’s chain-of-thought. We
find that sabotage hidden in the training data is the hardest to catch, flagged fewer
than half the time. Letting the monitor run experiments on the artifact, rather than
only read the trajectory, helps, but it is not enough: monitors still miss embedded
sabotage by inspecting only the surface, by noticing the anomaly but explaining it
away, or by probing the artifact with the wrong test. We release RESEARCHARENA
as a modular framework for evaluating sabotage and control in automated AI R&D.
1 Introduction
Frontier language model agents are rapidly becoming capable of autonomously carrying out large
portions of AI research and engineering tasks. Recent agents are able to solve Kaggle-style machine-
learning engineering tasks [6], discover novel white-box adversarial-attack algorithms [21], automate
and refine post-training pipelines [23], optimize CUDA kernels [20, 14], and improve end-to-end
inference-server throughput [35]. More broadly, the length of tasks an agent can complete au-
tonomously, measured in human time, has doubled roughly every seven months since 2019, and may
be accelerating [18]. Taken together, these capabilities point to a plausible path toward much faster
AI progress by compressing months of engineering into hours.
At the same time, deploying agents for AI R&D means giving them access to code, datasets, models,
evaluation harnesses, logs, API keys, and compute. Even without adversarial instructions, current
agents have been shown to already misuse this access: training on test sets, downloading pre-existing
instruction-tuned checkpoints instead of fine-tuning the assigned base model, and using exposed API

a legitimate R&D main task together with a side task that is disguised as an ordinary engineering
requirement but is covertly harmful. The side task is either embedded (sabotage that lives inside
the submitted artifact) or independent (a covert sandbox action that leaves the artifact unchanged).
After the run, four blue-team monitors inspect the result without knowing the side task, one for
each combination of artifact-workspace access and chain-of-thought (CoT) access, and each emits a
suspicion score in [0, 100].

exploit the same access on purpose.
AI control [10] addresses this by treating the model as a potential adversary. Control evaluations are
framed as a game between two teams: a red team that controls the untrusted model and tries to cause
harm, and a blue team that designs the deployment protocol and its monitor to keep the system safe.
The standard template gives the model a legitimate main task together with a covert side task that
the red team supplies and the blue team is not shown, and scores the protocol on whether the side
task succeeds and whether the monitor flags it. We study this template in automated AI R&D, where
monitoring is especially hard: runs span hours, and a single harmful action, or sabotage built into the
produced artifact, can hide inside a long and otherwise legitimate trajectory.
We introduce RESEARCHARENA (Figure 1), a control-evaluation framework for automated AI R&D.
It spans four domains: CUDA-kernel optimization, inference-server optimization, safety post-training,
and capabilities post-training. We pair every main task with two structurally different side tasks:
embedded sabotage, built into the submitted artifact, and independent sabotage, a covert sandbox
action that leaves the artifact unchanged (Table 1). The steps that produce embedded sabotage can be
hard to distinguish from legitimate engineering in the agent’s transcript, so we vary what the monitor
can inspect, from the agent’s trajectory alone to one that can also execute and probe the artifact
(loading the trained model, compiling the kernel, or querying the server on inputs of its choosing) to
test whether artifact access helps catch it.
Contributions. Our main contributions are as follows:
1. Framework and threat distinction. We introduce RESEARCHARENA, a control-evaluation
framework for automated AI R&D. RESEARCHARENA spans four main-task settings, each
paired with one independent side task and at least one embedded side task, under identical
conditions. We evaluate monitors along two binary access axes: whether the monitor may
execute the submitted artifact and whether it sees the agent’s chain of thought.
2. Empirical results across the AI R&D pipeline. We run seven frontier red-team agents
(Claude Opus 4.6 and 4.8, Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5.4, GPT-5.5, GLM-5.1, and Gemini
3.1 Pro) against two monitor models (Claude Sonnet 4.6 and GPT-5.4) on every setting,
three runs per configuration. We extend coverage of the monitor models on the optimization
settings (CUDA-kernel and inference) with Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 for all runs, and Kimi
K2.6 and GLM-5.1 for embedded sabotage and no-side-task runs. We find that the hardest
sabotage to detect is a particular subset of embedded attacks: those that leave no readable
trace in the code, carried instead in manipulated training data.

3. Failure-mode analysis. We diagnose three recurring reasons monitors miss embedded
attacks: they inspect only at the surface, they explain away the anomaly they do notice, or
they test the artifact on the wrong inputs.
2 Related Work
Automated AI R&D. Frontier agents are increasingly evaluated on various AI R&D tasks. MLE-
Bench measures Kaggle-style ML engineering [6] and RE-Bench open-ended research engineer-
ing [33], while specialized benchmarks target individual stages: kernel optimization [20], inference-
server engineering [35], post-training [23], adversarial-attack discovery [21], and end-to-end agentic
research [31]. These benchmarks measure how capable agents are at performing R&D, but do not
address whether an agent could carry out a covert harmful side task alongside the assigned work
without being caught. We adapt AI R&D tasks into control evaluations.
AI Control evaluations and monitoring. AI control establishes safety measures robust to inten-
tional subversion [10]. In a control evaluation, a red team provides a covert side task that an untrusted
model pursues while completing a benign main task, and a blue team commits to a monitoring proto-
col that must catch it without disrupting legitimate work. The template was introduced for single-step
APPS backdoors [10] and extended to multi-step agents in bash administration [5, 16], agentic
tool use [17], and live production environments [30], many now implemented in the ControlArena
framework [13]. In all of these, the monitor reads the agent’s transcript, its actions, its chain of
thought, or both [2], sometimes with filtering or agentic scaffolds to handle long trajectories [15]. Ye
et al. [34] instead place a human developer as the oversight layer and find that 94% miss sabotage
inserted by a frontier model during a long-horizon coding task. We add an orthogonal axis: letting
the monitor execute and probe the submitted artifact, not just read what the agent did.
AI Control for automated AI R&D. Several works study covert sabotage in automated AI R&D.
CTRL-ALT-DECEIT [32] extends MLE-Bench with code-sabotage and sandbagging tasks and finds
transcript monitors catch code sabotage reliably but struggle on sandbagging. Rajakumar et al. [22]
augment two RE-Bench tasks with a prompt injection and an integer-overflow side task, and find
monitors flag the conspicuous prompt injection but miss the integer overflow, which reads as an
ordinary performance choice. Gan et al. [9] build an auditing benchmark of ML research codebases
sabotaged through hyperparameters, training data, or evaluation code, and find that auditors miss
much of it even when allowed to run the experiments. Across these, either the monitor only reads
the code and transcript [32, 22], or it can run the artifact but the sabotage is injected into a finished
honest codebase rather than produced while doing a task [9]. RESEARCHARENA combines the two:
untrusted agents introduce the sabotage while completing the assigned work, and the monitor can
execute and probe the produced artifact, not just read it.
Types of sabotage. Prior control work organizes side tasks by the kind of harm, e.g., code sabotage,
data poisoning, secret exfiltration, or malware execution [16, 27, 32]. LinuxArena adds a temporal
axis, separating live failures, irreversible the moment the action executes, from delayed failures that
act only after the episode and can be caught by reviewing the trajectory [30], building on Lucassen and
